title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - All Critical Infrastructure
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: Refrigeration hack hit about 700 French supermarkets; Forescout now counts nearly 13,000 exposed refrigeration control services worldwide
items.content_text: On 22 October Forescout reported 12,976 internet-exposed refrigeration management services in 99 countries — the class of web-managed controller attackers forced into continuous defrost at French supermarkets on the nights of 11–13 October. France’s finance minister put the toll at about 700 stores, including Carrefour, E.Leclerc, Intermarché and Monoprix; the Paris prosecutor says fires also resulted and is investigating with ANSSI. CERT-FR names Danfoss AK-SC and AK-SM controllers plus Copeland and Dixell XWEB, and its 16 October revision says the campaigns are probably still under way. Most affected units are end-of-life, and the EU Cyber Resilience Act will not compel fixes for them. No actor, CVE or entry route has been named, and no new attack nights have been reported since 13 October.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Forescout Vedere Labs (22 Oct 2026); CERT-FR alert CERTFR-2026-ALE-012 (v1 12 Oct, v2 13 Oct adding Copeland and Dixell XWEB, v3 16 Oct); The Record (20 Oct 2026); SecurityWeek (15 Oct 2026); AP via News4JAX (13 Oct 2026); Danfoss statement (12 Oct 2026)
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Attacks on the nights of 11–13 Oct 2026, none reported since; latest CERT-FR revision 16 Oct 2026 (campaigns probably still ongoing); updated 22 Oct 2026 with Forescout exposure data — investigation ongoing

items.title: Ukraine’s CERT-UA warns that attackers are taking over Dahua surveillance cameras and recorders
items.content_text: In a warning issued late in the week before The Record reported it on 26 October, CERT-UA said attackers had compromised internet-connected Dahua cameras and network video recorders, changed their settings and created unauthorized user accounts. They appear to abuse Dahua’s Easy4IP cloud remote-access feature: serial numbers follow predictable patterns, so cloud-connected units can be found by guessing and then opened with weak or default passwords or through outdated firmware; CERT-UA flagged the 2021 authentication bypasses CVE-2021-33044 and CVE-2021-33045. The agency did not say how many devices were hit, when, by whom, or which organizations own them. Cameras and recorders are common on plant perimeters, substations, pumping stations and terminals, and they often sit on the same networks as operations gear, so an exposed unit is both a surveillance risk and a possible foothold (editorial assessment).

items.title: The FortiOS flaw behind Unit 42’s Peerstitch case enters CISA KEV, after a FortiManager compromise exposed more than 500 managed firewalls
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2025-61624, a FortiOS command-line path-traversal flaw, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 16 October, two days after Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 described its use. In that case attackers exploited FortiManager (CVE-2024-47575) at a telecommunications managed service provider and took configuration and credential material for more than 500 managed FortiGate firewalls; Unit 42 calls this exposure, not confirmed intrusion into those customers’ networks. They then used CVE-2025-61624 to get root on managed FortiGates and drop the Peerstitch loader, and wiped logs and rogue accounts. Unit 42 tracks the cluster as CL-STA-0954 (also UNC5820); it overlaps with suspected nation-state intrusions, but no state is named. Fortinet fixed the flaw in April and rates it Medium because it needs privileged access. The CVE record also lists Siemens RUGGEDCOM APE1808 as affected, through Siemens advisory SSA-975644.

items.title: Ransomware crews are now using the PAN-OS GlobalProtect authentication bypass to get past MFA and into networks, including utilities, energy and manufacturers
items.content_text: Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 updated its brief on 19–20 October to report that ransomware operators are exploiting CVE-2026-0257, an authentication bypass in the PAN-OS GlobalProtect portal and gateway, to start VPN sessions without valid credentials and bypass MFA. Unit 42 ties the activity to Spikey Scorpius (Qilin) and Tarnished Scorpius (Inc), and public reporting also names Settra. Exploitation was first seen in June, after a proof of concept appeared on 29 May; the flaw was fixed in May and added to CISA’s KEV catalog on 29 May. Targeted sectors include utilities and energy, manufacturing, and transportation and logistics. After entry the crews use remote-management tools, move over RDP and SMB, and in one case pivoted to vCenter, disabled security controls on ESXi hosts and dumped credentials from a domain controller’s virtual disk. No OT impact is reported.

items.title: CISA, the FBI and partners warn that SafePay ransomware has hit at least 600 organizations since August 2024
items.content_text: Advisory AA26-293A, issued on 20 October by CISA, the FBI and the US Secret Service with Germany’s LKA Rheinland-Pfalz, the UK National Crime Agency and the North West Regional Organised Crime Unit, says SafePay has hit at least 600 organizations from multiple critical-infrastructure sectors in North America, South America, Europe and Australia. Entry is usually through exposed or brute-forced credentials, phished accounts, VPN logins from Mullvad addresses and automated exploitation of edge-device flaws; the group then steals data, deletes shadow copies, resets network-attached storage that holds backups and moves with tools such as WinRM, PsExec and RDP. The advisory carries indicators and ATT&CK mappings for activity from November 2024 to August 2026. It names no victims, and reporting on it describes no OT, energy or water impact, so the OT risk here is the usual one: a ransomware crew reaching the IT network that plant systems depend on.

items.title: Albert Heijn restarts home deliveries after the Ahold Delhaize cyberattack; the group confirms malicious activity, and stores stayed open
items.content_text: Albert Heijn restarted grocery home deliveries on 23 October at about a third of normal capacity, nearly two weeks after Ahold Delhaize took systems offline on 12 October across most of its brands in Europe and the US; it expected to deliver all orders again from 28 October (not yet confirmed), and Dutch police are investigating the attack as a criminal case (NL Times). In its latest statement, on 19 October, the group said outside experts had confirmed “malicious actions of others”, that it had notified the Dutch NCSC and filed a police report, and that it had no evidence so far that sensitive data was taken; stores stayed open throughout. Ahold Delhaize USA’s banner websites and apps came back online on 20 October (Grocery Dive). The group has issued no cyber update since 19 October; its third-quarter results are due on 4 November. Albert Heijn said its distribution centres had to be restarted on 13–14 October (as reported by NL Times). No attacker or ransomware claim is known. This was an IT-side attack that disrupted logistics, not a confirmed OT compromise, and the Dutch NCSC saw no link to the French refrigeration attack.

items.title: A third Citrix NetScaler zero-day is exploited, and a fourth critical flaw was patched on 9 October
items.content_text: Citrix has confirmed a third NetScaler zero-day under attack, days after patching two others that were exploited for weeks before disclosure, and on 9 October it shipped a fourth fix. The exploited trio is CVE-2026-88771, CVE-2026-88772 and CVE-2026-88779; the federal KEV deadline for the newest passed on 7 October. The earlier pair brought web shells, rogue admin accounts and stolen configurations, and patching does not evict an intruder. The new CVE-2026-107406 (CVSS v4.0 9.5) is a SAML memory overflow that could allow code execution; no exploitation is reported, but appliances patched last week need another upgrade. Shadowserver counts more than 20,000 internet-exposed NetScaler fingerprints. Because NetScaler often fronts remote access into plant networks, an unhunted appliance is a possible foothold toward OT.

items.title: Ivanti warns attackers chained three zero-day flaws, one still unpatched, to take root on fully patched Connect Secure VPNs
items.content_text: Ivanti disclosed on 13 October that a small number of customers were hit through a chain of three zero-day flaws that gave unauthenticated, root-level code execution on fully patched Connect Secure appliances. Volexity, which found it while investigating a customer incident, dates its case to 3 October (other researchers saw activity from 1 October) and tracks a previously undocumented actor, UTA0576. The intruders stole domain credentials stored on the appliance, searched Active Directory for LAPS passwords and BitLocker recovery keys, sprayed passwords and scanned internal networks, but left no web shell or backdoor. Volexity judges, with low confidence, that the group is financially motivated, and, with medium confidence, that it uses AI models for exploit development. Fixes cover two of the flaws (CVE-2026-104935); the third, a privilege-escalation bug, is still unpatched. VPN gateways like this commonly sit at the IT/OT boundary.

items.title: The “Blue Initiative” maritime coalition launches a public repository of IT and OT vulnerabilities for shipping
items.content_text: Cydome, Rakuten Maritime, Bureau Veritas, ClassNK and MTS-ISAC, working together as the Blue Initiative, have launched the Maritime Vulnerabilities Repository, a public database limited to IT and OT vulnerabilities relevant to the maritime sector (Infosecurity Magazine, 26 October). Researchers from Cydome and the other partners review proposed entries before publication, and entries are published only once a patch is available. Users can filter by equipment or vendor, read analyst notes and subscribe to alerts. SecurityWeek, which describes the database as free and covering ship and port systems, reports nearly 30,000 entries, more than 580 of them known to be exploited and only 37 tied to maritime-specific products; those figures appear only in its report and could not be verified. It is a resource launch, not a new threat report, but it gives vessel and terminal operators a maritime-specific way to prioritize patching (editorial assessment).
tags: Resource — public database of maritime-relevant IT/OT vulnerabilities (the Maritime Vulnerabilities Repository), launched by the Blue Initiative coalition by 26 October 2026

items.title: Booz Allen: frontier AI models went from a perimeter breach to a control-zone action in just over 16 minutes in a lab test
items.content_text: Booz Allen’s 8 October report describes tests in its isolated OT lab in Chantilly, Virginia, modelled on a manufacturing facility. Frontier models from several unnamed vendors achieved every test objective across eight controlled scenarios, going from a perimeter compromise to energising an output on a controller in just over 16 minutes, with a human required to approve every exploit and physical action. One agent found a robotic arm’s API, gained admin access and moved the arm, and a SCADA gateway holding live authenticated sessions to 14 devices gave the models a ready path. Some controls held: one controller rejected a stop command, and local-control mode blocked a remote motor start. Booz Allen calls the results preliminary; some known flaws were left unpatched on purpose and no zero-days were developed. Its Kyle Miller told Dark Reading that removing the approval step would likely have roughly halved the time.

items.title: AI-agent ransomware toolkit “Phantom” used edge and remote-access flaws, with industrial and manufacturing firms the largest group of targets
items.content_text: SOCRadar researchers (report published 20 October, updated 23 October, and covered by The Hacker News on 23 October) found an exposed server showing affiliates of the INC and The Gentlemen ransomware groups running intrusions through an AI-agent framework called Phantom, with a human operator writing prompts and reviewing each step. According to the operator’s own records, entry came through internet-facing systems such as FortiClient EMS, SimpleHelp, cPanel and VPN gateways, and one reused password opened VPN, backup, remote-management and security platforms. SOCRadar lists 62 named target organisations, 36 of them in the US, with industrial and manufacturing firms the largest group (about 16%, roughly ten organisations); four appeared on leak sites. The activity is IT-side data theft and extortion; the report describes no access to controllers or SCADA, but the same edge entry points and reused credentials are what an attacker needs to reach OT-adjacent networks.

items.title: Accenture, Dragos and SANS launch a $10 million programme to put OT monitoring in up to 500 small utilities
items.content_text: The Community Cyber Resilience Foundation, announced on 20 October by Accenture, Dragos and the SANS Institute with Elastic providing technology support, offers free OT security help to small water, wastewater, electric and natural gas utilities with under $100 million in annual revenue. Dragos describes it as a US programme; the foundation’s own site also mentions Canada. Participants get the Dragos Platform, Neighborhood Keeper and OT-CERT; Accenture assessment, deployment and ongoing support; SANS training with GIAC certification; and hardware funding where needed. About $10 million in funding and services covers a first phase of up to 500 utilities, on top of the 100-plus already in Dragos’s Community Defense Program, and enrollment “opens soon”. It is a resource announcement, not a threat report, but it reaches the small operators that have struggled to fund OT monitoring (editorial assessment).

items.title: Siemens confirms a Software Center flaw is being exploited to deliver malware, and CISA adds it to the KEV catalog
items.content_text: Siemens first published CVE-2026-110936 on 15 October and on 19 October confirmed it is being exploited. Software Center, the tool engineers use to install and update Siemens software, did not restrict where it searches for helper DLLs, so attackers paired a genuine, validly signed copy with their own malicious libraries in an installer package. Siemens ties the activity to the “Romulus” multi-platform ClickFix campaign, which tricks users into running pasted commands, and names no final malware family. It says no Siemens system, product or update channel was breached, to its knowledge. Version 4.0.9.8 fixes the flaw, and installed copies update on next start. CISA added the flaw to KEV on 20 October with a 3 November deadline and has republished Siemens’ advisory as ICSA-26-295-03. Exploitation needs local access and a user who runs the lure, so engineering workstations running Siemens tooling are the exposure.

items.title: PHP2Shell is in CISA KEV and Palo Alto reports attacks on exposed PAN-OS management interfaces; Siemens, Schneider and ABB list affected OT products, and Schneider now has a Control Engineering fix
items.content_text: PHP2Shell is a pair of unauthenticated remote-code-execution flaws in PHP (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, CVSS v4.0 9.2 per the PHP Group) fixed on 21 October in PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12. Exploitation attempts began on 17 October, and over 24–25 October researchers at Perplexity, backed by Expel’s Marcus Hutchins, confirmed working remote code execution against a honeypot. CISA, which had published a SIGMA detection rule on 23 October, added both flaws to its KEV catalog on 26 October with a 29 October federal deadline, without describing the activity. Palo Alto Networks’ advisory, raised to Critical on 27 October and updated on 28 October, reports active exploitation targeting PAN-OS management interfaces exposed to the internet on PA-Series, VM-Series and Panorama (web UI and XML API; GlobalProtect is not affected); it names no victims, and hotfixes are rolling out 21–30 October. That reaches OT directly: Siemens’ SSA-566512 lists RUGGEDCOM APE1808 units running PAN-OS as affected, with remediation through Siemens customer support plus Palo Alto’s workarounds. Schneider’s bulletin SESB-2026-295-01, revised to v2.0.0 on 26 October, says remediation is now available for EcoStruxure Control Engineering (applied automatically when the VM can reach the debian.org and sury.org repositories; otherwise request a patch from Schneider support); Security Expert is fixed in 1.48.4.0 and LINEoptimize is handled through ProLeiT support. ABB lists APROL R 4.4-65 and earlier, with patches planned for 26 and 29 October, and ABB MES installations that use DokuWiki (update PHP or shut DokuWiki down). Rockwell (SD1802, 23 October) has confirmed no affected products while its review continues, and Siemens lists 31 software products and 20 Smart Infrastructure products as not affected, with its evaluation ongoing. No victim organisation has been named and no compromise of an OT product has been reported. Sophos and Unit 42 withdrew earlier reports of successful exploitation, including Unit 42’s link to a European government agency compromise, and CYFIRMA’s tie between a scanning campaign and North Korea is a single-vendor assessment. Software that bundles PHP is easy to miss in IT patch sweeps (editorial assessment), so ask OT vendors directly.

items.title: October ICS fixes: critical ICONICS GENESIS64 flaws and a WAGO controller bug join Siemens, Rockwell and ABB, and some Siemens flaws still have no fix
items.content_text: On 22 October CISA republished Siemens’ 13 October advisories (ICSA-26-295-02 to -18): fixes are still pending for the S7 PLC web server, the S7-1500 MFP Linux subsystems and WinCC V7.5, and none is planned for APOGEE MBC/MEC. CISA’s 20 October batch covered WAGO controller firmware (CVE-2026-80466, CVSS v3.1 8.8: a low-privileged user can inject commands that run as root; fixed in 4.10.0/FW32) and Moxa’s AIG-302 edge gateway (hard-coded key CVE-2026-109813, v3.1 8.1 / v4.0 8.6; fixed in 1.4.1). Mitsubishi Electric’s 15 October advisory fixes an authentication bypass (CVE-2026-16436, CVSS v3.1 8.1) and over-permissive DCOM defaults (CVE-2026-16438, v3.1 9.1) across ICONICS GENESIS64, GENESIS, Hyper Historian and related products; MC Works64, GENESIS32 and BizViz get no fix, and Mitsubishi advises replacing them. CISA republished the advisory on 27 October as ICSA-26-300-02. Earlier in the month Rockwell fixed a critical 1732E ArmorBlock admin-takeover flaw and ABB a dynovaPRO password-reset flaw. None is reported exploited.

items.title: BeyondTrust patches a Remote Support zero-day exploited since late August by a suspected China-nexus espionage actor
items.content_text: BeyondTrust has fixed CVE-2026-102764, an authentication bypass in self-hosted Remote Support appliances (version 26.2.3 and earlier) that lets an unprivileged remote attacker perform file operations. Mandiant and Google’s threat-intelligence group link the exploitation to a suspected state-sponsored espionage actor they track as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221); CrowdStrike calls it Warp Panda. After getting in, the intruders used web shells, escalated to root, wiped logs and harvested stored credentials for lateral movement. SaaS customers were patched on 8 October; self-hosted customers must patch themselves. Shadowserver counts more than 1,400 exposed instances, and Google expects opportunistic exploitation to follow. No victims are named, and none is reported in critical infrastructure. Integrators and OEMs often use this class of tool for vendor access to plants, so its owners should check it. CISA added the flaw to its KEV catalog on 16 October with a three-day deadline (19 October, now passed). BeyondTrust, as the CVE numbering authority, scores it CVSS v4.0 9.3.

items.title: Coast Guard issues NVIC 02-26 on maritime cybersecurity plans and IT/OT risk assessments, with a 16 July 2027 deadline
items.content_text: The US Coast Guard released NVIC 02-26, a companion to its maritime cybersecurity rule, for operators of US-flagged vessels, port facilities and Outer Continental Shelf facilities regulated under the Maritime Transportation Security Act. It explains how to name a cybersecurity officer, complete a cyber risk assessment and write a Cybersecurity Plan for Coast Guard approval; all three are due by 16 July 2027. The approach is performance-based: operators choose how to meet each requirement, but must back claims with documentation and observable evidence, and a plan that only restates the regulation must also explain how it is met. Penetration testing is not needed for the first submission but is expected periodically over five-year renewal cycles, with attention to OT safety. Enclosures cover plan development, a sample officer letter, penetration-testing guidance and an optional NIST CSF method for scoping IT and OT systems.

items.title: OT-ISAC maps Asia-Pacific cyber rules for critical infrastructure; Japan’s common standards took effect 1 October
items.content_text: OT-ISAC’s APAC OT/CI Cyber Policy Intelligence Report, published on 20 October and summarised by Industrial Cyber, sorts 2026 Asia-Pacific policy changes into binding rules, nonbinding guidance, drafts and future-dated measures. According to Industrial Cyber’s summary, Japan’s Common Cybersecurity Standards for Critical Infrastructure took effect on 1 October 2026 and Singapore issued its 2026 Critical Information Infrastructure Code of Practice on 29 July. It is a policy summary, not a new requirement or an advisory, and operators with plants in the region should check which items apply to them.

items.title: Centrii warns low-impact grid sites to prove NERC CIP-003-9 vendor remote access controls before auditors ask
items.content_text: In a 26 October analysis, compliance firm Centrii says CIP-003-9, in effect since 1 April 2026, now requires owners of low-impact bulk electric system assets that allow vendor remote access to have three processes: identify vendor remote access, disable it, and detect known or suspected malicious communications tied to it. The standard does not define “vendor”, and ReliabilityFirst expects auditors to read it broadly, including staff augmentation. Centrii flags records as the weak spot: evidence must be kept for three calendar years, audits of low-impact requirements can reach back six, and the proof is often scattered across email, equipment-maker support portals and contractor systems. The owner stays accountable even when operations are outsourced. Centrii recommends one named person to approve each vendor access path, one to disable it and one place for records. This is a vendor’s compliance commentary, not a regulator statement.
